cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Welcome to Explainopolis — a map that explains how it was made. I'm Maya, I'll be your guide.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: And I'm Owen. I'll ask what you would ask. So — why a map? What's wrong with the document?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Nothing, except that nobody reads it. A report keeps its argument in tables, caveats and page forty-seven. These three are real: a materials-science chapter, an arXiv paper, and a CEO's project canvas.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Three very different documents. One tool for all of them?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: The same kit. This plaza is the evidence. The paper ran to about twenty-three thousand words; its map has thirty-eight buildings and a nine-stop tour.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: The goal out there says minutes, not pages. Let's see you earn it.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Let me guess. You paste the paper into a chatbot and it draws a city?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Not quite. A discovery agent reads the source and proposes how to map it — the axis, the districts, the landmarks — on a single page.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: And who checks that page?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: A person. That's the first gate, and it's cheap: you argue about one page before anything is built. Then an architect agent turns the approved profile into a city spec — what exists, what flows where, what blocks what. No coordinates.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Agents write numbers. Agents get numbers wrong.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Which is why the second gate is here: a human review, and a provenance file that separates what the source says, what we recounted, and what is only a choice of the map. On the paper's map it records the one place where the map follows the authors' own audit instead of the printed text.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: So that red flag on the spec is a limit you admit, not a bug you hide.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Exactly. Every map here draws its limits where they act.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Your turn. Show me where a human checks the agents' work.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Exactly. Agents draft, a person approves, and the provenance file keeps the receipts.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Close. The gates are here: the one-page profile, and the human review with its provenance file.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: From here on, nothing is guessed. The compiler reads the spec, places every building, routes every road, and works out the cameras for this tour.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Deterministic? Same spec, same city?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Same spec, same city. About fifteen hundred lines of plain Python. It refuses a spec with a broken reference, and every change is rendered headless before it ships.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Still, this city is a lot. I'd lose my manager by district two.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Then switch. Same spec, drawn as a metro map: one line per district, and the interchanges are where the story changes lines.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: The same file? Not a second drawing?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: The same file. Click an interchange and it tells you why it's there. One spec, every view — that's the goal of this district.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: And the catch?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Big districts still need positions by hand. It's marked, right there on the compiler.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Here's my real question. Who is talking right now?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: We are — but neither of us was recorded. This conversation is a script in the same spec, and deckcast turned it into voices.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: deckcast being?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: A small tool that compiles a narration script into voiced clips, caches them, and times every line. Those timings are why the map moves exactly when I say — here.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Neat. So this tour is level one. What are two and three?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Level two: the map asks you — you've met it already — and you answer with a click. Level three: you simply ask, out loud, and an agent answers from the map's own knowledge and flies the camera for you.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: A live agent in a live demo. What could possibly go wrong.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: The network. That's why it's marked as a limit — and why levels one and two need no live connection at all.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: Last question, and it's the one a jury asks. Is anyone actually using this?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Yes. The materials-science chapter, the arXiv paper, and a real code base — a gear's spec traced line by line into its code — are public maps you can open today.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: And the third one?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: A CEO's view of a live project. Private, because it names people and risks — same kit, kept local.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: And deckcast?

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: Two decks narrated end to end, one with a link where you can talk to the agent.

cues.speaker: owen
cues.text: So the thing explaining itself is built exactly like the things it explains.

cues.speaker: maya
cues.text: That's the point. One spec, a compiler and a script — and a document nobody reads becomes a place you can walk through. And a place you can ask: press the Ask button, bottom right, and talk to me.
